correctness.rationale: The compact symmetric square S of the geometric graph has the collision diagonal as a closed subpolyhedron. For this compact polyhedral pair the open complement's locally finite homology is the pair homology, naturally for homeomorphisms. Homotopies of graph maps do induce homotopies of compact pairs even when no map of configuration spaces is defined. On a bouquet, the absolute symmetric square has one vertex, single-petal and diagonal degree-one generators a_i and d_i, same-petal triangles with boundary ±(2a_i−d_i), and product tori with zero boundary in degree two. Thus the absolute H₁ is freely generated by a_i; the diagonal map is twice the single-coordinate inclusion there. The latter map on homology is independent of basepoint by path-connectedness. The diagonal map is injective on the free cycle lattice, and both spaces are connected, so the pair sequence gives H₁=V/2V and H₂=H₂(S). Cross products pushed through the symmetric quotient are skew by the degree-one exchange sign. Repeated products vanish because the two-dimensional polyhedron S has torsion-free H₂. Different petals map with degree one onto the oriented mixed-cell generators, proving the integral exterior-square basis and naturality; bouquet homotopy equivalence carries this to all allowed graphs. All other degrees vanish, also for b₁=0 or 1 with the obvious empty sets of generators. The trace formula is the ordinary exterior-square trace identity.
residual_risks: The statement is for constant coefficients and geometric, locally finite configuration homology. The finite script checks ranks, small Smith samples and rational Lefschetz traces; naturality and the integral action are proved by the compact pair and cross-product maps, not by those tests.

evidence: Gugnin gives integral additive bases and multiplicative generators modulo torsion for symmetric powers of a broader class of spaces. Kallel–Salvatore show that the symmetric power of a circle bouquet is homotopy equivalent to the corresponding skeleton of the torus, in particular the two-skeleton for n=2; graphs reduce to bouquets for this absolute calculation. Khan's group theorem for simple connected graphs also covers the geometric spaces of nonsimple finite graphs by subdivision.
broader_coverage.reasoning: The two-skeleton of the product CW torus has zero cellular differentials, so its degree-one and degree-two homology and cohomology are free. Thus Gugnin's quotient-by-torsion qualification is harmless here. Taking n=2 and only degree-one generators gives the full absolute integral exterior algebra in degrees one and two, naturally; the bouquet equivalence is only required for torsion-freeness, not for any choice of basis in the natural maps.

evidence: Write U=H¹(G;ℤ)=V*. With q:G²→S, Gugnin gives q*χ(a)=a⊗1+1⊗a. The natural χ identifies U with H¹(S). Cup products χ(a)χ(b) form the exterior-square basis in degree two (q* sends them to a⊗b−b⊗a). The diagonal pulls χ(a) back to 2a. Absolute H₁ and H₂ are free by the torus-skeleton theorem. Hence dualizing gives H₁(S)=V with diagonal 2, and H₂(S)=Λ²V. Pairing χ(a)χ(b) with q_*(α×β) produces a(α)b(β)−b(α)a(β), so the integral identification is precisely the one in the finding, with no missing factor of two.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: All maps in the pair sequence are natural under graph homeomorphisms. Injectivity of 2 on V and H₂(G)=0 give H₂^{BM}=Λ²V, and connectedness makes H₁^{BM}=coker(2)=V/2V. The trace is an immediate algebraic identity for Λ². This is a full statement-level implication, not just agreement of ranks or general background that leaves an integral action to be determined.

evidence: The geometric configuration is exactly Sym²(G) minus its diagonal. Khan's theorem gives the graded untwisted groups. Gugnin's generators pull back under the quotient map to the two-coordinate sums of degree-one classes and their products give the integral degree-two basis modulo torsion.
equivalent_formulations.reasoning: The canonical homology formulation is dual to the natural degree-one and degree-two symmetric-square cohomology identifications plus the diagonal cokernel. The sign-twisted divided square is a genuinely different formulation with different coefficients, not a substitute for the untwisted argument.

originality.rationale: The claim is correct but a direct consequence of older results on the symmetric-product cohomology ring and the known Borel–Moore model, together with the ordinary relative exact sequence. Specifically, for n=2 Gugnin's integral generator and basis theorem gives natural H¹ and H² identifications, and the diagonal is twice the identity in degree one by pullback of its explicit generators. The Kallel–Salvatore graph result eliminates torsion and supplies free absolute homology in these degrees. Duality and the relative sequence then give both claimed integral automorphism modules and exactly the claimed cross-product identification. The failure is this demonstrated implication, not the absence of a new search hit or a claim that Khan writes down the integral actions explicitly.
residual_risks: The search does not settle who first wrote down the relative module formulas verbatim. The failure rests on constructive implication of inspected older theorems, not on an assertion of literal prior wording.

value.rationale: The canonical identifications are a useful way of presenting the known groups, but the claimed advance consists entirely of specializing a known integral symmetric-product ring theorem, taking duals and applying the natural exact sequence with the two-coordinate diagonal. Neither an additional invariant nor a new obstruction or surprising boundary survives that implication. The trace formula and extension to subdivided graph models are routine consequences of the same calculation. The record is an accurate exposition, not an independently needed unknown invariant or substantial new classification under this standard.
residual_risks: This assessment does not discount possible value of different coefficient systems, ordinary configuration homology, or more-particle representations, none of which the frozen theorem claims.
